title: In Tayba a Trace of the Messenger Remains
intro: Hassan ibn Thabit wrote this elegy for the Prophet after his death in 11 AH (632 CE). It is the first of his elegies that Ibn Hisham gives in the Sira after the account of the death, on the authority of Abu Zayd al-Ansari, and later books of the Prophet's life repeat it. It opens in the old manner of the ode, at the traces of an abandoned dwelling, but these traces are the Prophet's in Medina: his pulpit, his mosque, his rooms and then his grave, where the poet weeps and calls down blessings on the grave and the land that holds it, and recalls the mourners going home with revelation cut off from them. He then remembers the Prophet's guidance, mercy and forgiveness and his care for his people, until death's arrow struck while they were still in that light, and Medina and Mecca were left desolate; he bids his own eye weep. He ends with the Prophet's virtues, unmatched by any who have died, the nobility of his line, and the hope of being his neighbour in Paradise. The poet was the Prophet's own, who defended him in verse in Medina.

translation: In Tayba a trace of the Messenger remains, a dwelling place,
still bright, though traces fade and crumble.
1.sharh: The elegy opens with the old motif of the abandoned campsite, where poets stopped to weep over the traces of tents long gone. This trace is the Prophet's house in Medina, and unlike other ruins it does not fade.

translation: The signs of a hallowed house are not wiped away,
where stands the pulpit the Guide used to climb,
2.sharh: Ayat, “signs”, are landmarks, and the word is also the one for the verses of the Quran, which came down in this house and were recited there. From the pulpit the Prophet preached.

translation: clear signs and lasting landmarks,
and a home with a place of prayer, a mosque.
3.sharh: The Prophet's rooms adjoined his mosque in Medina, so the poet sees house and mosque as a single dwelling, its landmarks still plain to see.

translation: There are the rooms in whose midst came down
a light from God to see by, kindled bright.
4.sharh: The light is the revelation, which came down in those rooms. “Kindled” makes it a fire lit in the dark, the kind travellers steered by at night.

translation: Landmarks whose signs have not been effaced with time:
decay came to them, and their signs grow new.
5.sharh: Ruins wear away with time; these renew themselves. Decay comes to them as it comes to every dwelling, but their signs grow fresh instead of fading.

translation: There I knew the Messenger's trace and the place he lived,
and a grave where the one who laid him down hid him in the earth.
6.sharh: He knows the house as a poet knows an old campsite, by its traces, and beside it he finds the grave. From the Prophet's life the elegy turns to his death.

translation: There I stayed weeping for the Messenger, and eyes
wept with me, and my own lids gave twice as much.
7.sharh: Others wept with him, and his own eyes shed twice their tears: his loss is greater than theirs, so their weeping cannot be enough for him.

translation: My soul recalls the Messenger's blessings, and I
cannot count them: my soul is left dazed,
8.sharh: His soul tries to count the Prophet's gifts to mankind and cannot finish; it stands bewildered, like a traveller who has lost the road.

translation: grief-stricken, worn thin by the loss of Ahmad,
and still it goes on counting his blessings.
9.sharh: Mourners used to recite the virtues of the dead one by one. His soul does the same with the Prophet's blessings, so that the counting itself becomes a lament.

translation: It has not reached a tenth of any of his merits,
and my soul can praise only some of what was in him.
10.sharh: After all this counting he has not reached a tenth of any single merit. To confess that he falls short is itself the highest praise.

translation: Long it stood, the eye shedding tears with all its strength,
over the mound of the grave where Ahmad lies.
11.sharh: Calling the grave a talal, the word for the ruins at which the old odes begin, ties it back to the traces of the opening lines: this is the ruin he has come to weep at.

translation: Blessed are you, grave of the Messenger, and blessed
the land where the rightly guided, the unerring, rests.
12.sharh: He speaks to the grave itself and blesses it, and then the whole land around it, which is blessed because the Prophet now rests there.

translation: And blessed the hollow in you entrusted with one so pure,
covered over with flat stones, set one on another.
13.sharh: Flat stones were laid over the niche in which the body rested, before the earth was poured in. The pure one lies within, and the stones keep him.

translation: Hands pour the earth on him, and eyes their tears,
and at this the lucky stars have set.
14.sharh: One verb, “pour”, serves both the earth the hands throw and the tears the eyes shed. With the lucky stars gone down, the time of good fortune has ended.

translation: They buried forbearance, knowledge and mercy
the evening they heaped earth on him, unpillowed.
15.sharh: More than a body went into the grave: forbearance, knowledge and mercy went with it. He was laid in the bare earth with nothing under his head.

translation: They went home in grief, their Prophet no longer among them,
their backs and their arms gone weak.
16.sharh: Back and upper arm are the Arabic image of strength and support, as in the Quran (28:35), “We will strengthen your arm through your brother”. Without him the mourners have neither.

translation: They mourn one the heavens weep for on the day he died,
and the earth has wept for him; and people grieve more.
17.sharh: Heaven and earth weep for him, and men grieve more than both. The line answers the Quran (44:29), where heaven and earth did not weep for Pharaoh's people.

translation: Has the loss of any man ever equalled
the loss on the day Muhammad died?
18.sharh: The question needs no answer: no death can be set beside his. The next line gives the reason, that with it revelation ceased.

translation: That day the descent of revelation was cut off from them,
a light that had reached lowland and highland alike.
19.sharh: After his death revelation came down no more. Lowland and highland, Tihama by the sea and the plateau of Najd, are the two halves of Arabia: the light had reached all of it.

translation: He guided those who followed him to the Merciful,
saved them from the terror of disgrace, and showed them the way.
20.sharh: After the lines on his death, the portrait of the Prophet in his life begins: he led those who followed him to God, named here as al-Rahman, the Merciful.

translation: A leader who strove to guide them to the truth,
a true teacher: if they obeyed him, they were happy.
21.sharh: He led by teaching rather than force, and never misled them; their happiness lay in obeying him.

translation: Ready to forgive their slips, accepting their excuses,
and if they did good, God was more generous still.
22.sharh: He forgave those who did wrong, and those who did good God rewarded beyond anything they had done.

translation: And if a burden came that they could not carry,
it was he who made easy what had grown hard.
23.sharh: When a burden was too heavy for them, he eased it: he was their refuge in hardship, gentle with his people.

translation: So while they lived in God's grace, with a guide in their midst
by whom the clear road was found,
24.sharh: A dalil was the guide who led a caravan across the desert; the Prophet leads his people so. The sentence begun here breaks off, and is completed in line 27.

translation: grieved that they should stray from guidance,
eager that they keep straight and be guided,
25.sharh: The line echoes the Quran's description of the Prophet (9:128): “grievous to him is your suffering; he is eager for you, kind and merciful to the believers”.

translation: kind to them, not turning his wing
to one side, but tender to all, smoothing their way,
26.sharh: To lower one's wing is the Arabic image of tenderness, from a bird spreading its wing over its young, as in the Quran (26:215). His wing turned to no one side: his care took in all of them.

translation: while they were in that light, an arrow of death
flew to their light and struck home.
27.sharh: This completes the sentence of line 24: while they were still in that light, death struck. “Their light” is the Prophet himself.

translation: And he went back to God, praised,
wept for by the eyelids of those sent, and praised.
28.sharh: Mahmud and yuhmad, “praised” and “is praised”, echo his names Muhammad and Ahmad. Those sent are the angels, as many commentators read the word at the opening of Sura 77; they weep for him as men do.

translation: The lands of the sanctuary grew desolate,
now that the revelation they had known was gone,
29.sharh: The sanctuary lands are Mecca and Medina, both sacred: the lines that follow go from his grave in Medina to his birthplace in Mecca. The Sira's commentators take it as Mecca alone.

translation: deserted, but for the peopled grave where the lost one came as a guest,
mourned by al-Balat and the gharqad trees.
30.sharh: The grave is the one place still lived in, and the Prophet came to it as a guest comes to a host. The paved ground by his mosque and the trees of the cemetery mourn him.

translation: His mosque, and the places made desolate by his loss,
stand empty where he used to stand and sit.
31.sharh: His places in Medina stand where they were, empty of him: where he stood to pray and preach, and where he sat with his companions.

translation: And by the Great Jamra, there too stand desolate
his homes and yards, his dwelling and his birthplace.
32.sharh: The mourning moves to Mecca, where he was born and grew up, so that both his cities grieve alike.

translation: Weep for God's Messenger, my eye, shed tears,
and never let me see your tears run dry.
33.sharh: He turns to his own eye, as elegists often did. La a'rifannaki, “let me not find you”, is a set form of warning: never let your tears dry.

translation: How can you not weep for the giver of the blessing
that covers all mankind in its abundance?
34.sharh: The blessing is his mission, which reached all mankind and covers them like an ample garment.

translation: Be generous to him with your tears, and wail aloud
for the loss of one whose like will never be found.
35.sharh: To be generous with tears is an old Arabic image of weeping freely: the eye gives as a generous man gives, without holding back.

translation: Those who came before never lost a man like Muhammad,
nor will his like be lost until the Day of Rising,
36.sharh: No one before lost a man like him, and no one will until the end of time. The next five lines hang on this one: none more chaste, none truer, none nobler.

translation: none more chaste, none truer to pledge after pledge,
none readier with gifts unspoiled by reproach,
37.sharh: A gift spoiled by reproach is one the giver keeps reminding you of; his came with no such reminder.

translation: none more lavish with new wealth and old
when a generous man grows mean with what he has long held,
38.sharh: New wealth and old together mean everything he had. He gave it all away at the very moment when even generous men hold back.

translation: none of nobler clan among the houses when he named his line,
none of nobler forebears, lords of the valley of Mecca,
39.sharh: His clan and his forebears were the noblest of Quraysh, who lived in the valley bed of Mecca and ruled there.

translation: none with heights harder to reach, none set more firmly on high
on towering pillars of glory, raised ever higher,
40.sharh: His honour is a fortress on a mountain top that no one can climb, its pillars set firm.

translation: none firmer in branch among branches, or in root,
a stem the rain clouds nourished, so the stem is supple.
41.sharh: Far', “branch”, also means the noblest member of a clan. His lineage is a tree sound in root and branch, watered by the rain.

translation: A glorious Lord raised him from a child
and brought him to completion in the noblest virtues.
42.sharh: Rabbahu, “raised him”, echoes rabb, “Lord”: God Himself brought up the orphan (Quran 93:6), and perfected both his form and his character.

translation: The charge of the Muslims came to rest in his hand:
knowledge was not held back, judgement not found wanting.
43.sharh: “In his hand” means in his keeping. He did not withhold what he knew, and his judgement was never found at fault.

translation: I say this, and no one will find fault with my words
but one whose wits are far away, an outcast.
44.sharh: Only a man whose wits have wandered could fault such praise; the image is of a herdsman gone off with his camels, far from the camp.

translation: My love will not give up praising him;
through it, perhaps, I will live for ever in the Garden
45.sharh: Khuld, “eternity”, and akhludu, “I live for ever”, share a root: the Garden and his staying in it are named by one word.

translation: with the Chosen One; by it I hope to be his neighbour,
and to win that day I strive and toil.
46.sharh: The elegy ends in hope after weeping: parted from the Prophet in this world, he hopes to live beside him in the next.

1.1.1.head: طَيبَة
1.1.1.meaning: Tayba: Medina, “the good”, the name the Prophet gave it.

1.1.2.meaning: Rasm: a trace of a dwelling, the marks left on the ground after the tents are gone.

2.2.3.meaning: Al-Hadi: “the Guide”, the one who leads to the right way; here, the Prophet.

4.1.2.head: حُجُرات
4.1.2.meaning: Hujurat: rooms; the Prophet's wives' rooms beside his mosque, which give Sura 49 its name.

6.2.6.meaning: Mulhid: the one who lays the dead in the lahd, the niche of the grave.

7.1.5.head: أَسعَدَ
7.1.5.meaning: As'ada: helped someone weep, the word for joining another's mourning.

9.1.5.head: أَحمَد
9.1.5.meaning: Ahmad: one of the Prophet's names, from the same root as Muhammad, “praised”.

11.2.2.head: طَلَل
11.2.2.meaning: Talal: the standing remains of a dwelling, the ruins at which the old odes begin.

12.2.4-5.meaning: Al-rashid al-musaddad: “the rightly guided, the unerring”; the Prophet.

13.1.2.head: لَحد
13.1.2.meaning: Lahd: a niche cut into the side of a grave, in which the body is laid.

14.2.5.head: أَسعُد
14.2.5.meaning: As'ud: plural of sa'd, “good fortune”; the lucky stars, which the Arabs took as good omens.

15.1.3.head: حِلم
15.1.3.meaning: Hilm: forbearance, patience under provocation. The Sira prints hulm, “a dream”.

19.2.5-6.head: يَغور وَيُنجِد
19.2.5-6.meaning: Yaghuru wa-yunjidu: “goes down to the Ghawr and up to Najd”, the lowland and the highland; everywhere.

27.2.6.meaning: Muqsid: of an arrow, striking home and killing where it lands.

28.2.2-3.head: جَفن المُرسَلات
28.2.2-3.meaning: Jafn al-mursalat: “the eyelids of those sent”, the angels' eyes. The Sira has haqq, “the due of those sent”.

30.2.3.meaning: Al-Balat: “the pavement”, ground paved with stones between the Prophet's mosque and the market of Medina.

30.2.4.head: غَرقَد
30.2.4.meaning: Gharqad: boxthorn trees that grew in al-Baqi', the cemetery of Medina, called Baqi' al-Gharqad after them.

32.1.1-2.head: الجَمرَة الكُبرى
32.1.1-2.meaning: Al-Jamra al-Kubra: “the Great Jamra”, the pillar of al-Aqaba at Mina, outside Mecca, where pilgrims cast stones; here, Mecca and its surroundings.

32.1.4.meaning: Thamma: “there”, pointing to a place far off; not thumma, “then”.

38.1.3-4.meaning: Tarif and talid: wealth newly gained and wealth long held or inherited.

38.2.6.head: أَتلَدَ
38.2.6.meaning: Yutlad: gained long ago and kept. The Beirut edition has yutlid, “acquires of old”.

39.2.3.head: أَبطَحِيّ
39.2.3.meaning: Abtahi: of the abtah, the valley bed of Mecca where the leading clans of Quraysh lived.

40.1.2.head: ذِروات
40.1.2.meaning: Dhirwat: peaks, the highest points of a mountain.

41.2.5.meaning: Aghyad: supple and tender, bending easily, as a young green stem does.

44.2.4.head: عازِب
44.2.4.meaning: 'Azib: far off, absent; said of a herdsman who grazes his camels far from camp.

46.1.2.meaning: Al-Mustafa: “the Chosen One”, one of the Prophet's names.
